advisor.summary: Reg. §1.469-4 treats commonly controlled activities that form an 'appropriate economic unit' as a single activity for §469, relocating the material participation test: hours that fall short activity by activity can pass once pooled. A separate election under Reg. §1.469-9(g) lets a real estate professional treat all rental real estate interests as one activity. Both choices are structural and sticky — groupings bind future years, the Commissioner can regroup abusive combinations, and Rev. Proc. 2010-13 requires written disclosure of new groupings and changes. The election moves no dollars by itself; it governs which losses are currently usable and when suspended losses release, which is why the engine carries it as advisory at zero.
mechanics: Reg. §1.469-4(c) supplies the five-factor 'appropriate economic unit' standard — business similarity, common control, common ownership, geography, and interdependence. No single factor controls, and reasonable, consistently applied groupings are generally respected.
§469 measures material participation activity by activity, so combining related operations turns three failing 200-hour efforts into one passing 600-hour activity — the core planning effect.

Rental activities generally cannot be grouped with trade-or-business activities unless one side is insubstantial or ownership is proportionate (Reg. §1.469-4(d)), and real property rentals may never be grouped with personal property rentals.
The Reg. §1.469-9(g) aggregation is a distinct lever: a qualifying real estate professional tests material participation once across all rental real estate instead of property by property.

The cost side of the ledger: groupings bind future years under Reg. §1.469-4(e), the Commissioner may regroup to prevent avoidance under Reg. §1.469-4(f), and suspended losses release only on disposition of substantially all of the grouped activity under §469(g).
Rev. Proc. 2010-13 requires written disclosure of new groupings, additions, and regroupings; an undisclosed grouping risks treatment as separate activities at exam.

authority.note: The grouping rules: the appropriate-economic-unit standard, its five factors, and the limits on combining rentals with businesses.
The real estate professional's election to treat all rental real estate as a single activity when testing material participation.
Passive-activity definitions, the material participation standard the grouping re-scopes, and the entire-interest disposition rule the grouping enlarges.
Mandates written disclosure of new groupings, additions, and regroupings with the return.

requirements: A defensible economic unit — common control or ownership plus operational, geographic, or customer interdependence — documented in a grouping memo.
The Rev. Proc. 2010-13 disclosure statement filed with the return for every new grouping or change.
Forward consistency: the grouping is a binding structural choice, revisited only when the facts materially change.
For the §1.469-9(g) aggregation, real estate professional status established first and the election statement attached to a timely return.
risks: The leading exam theory is an undisclosed or economically hollow grouping: Reg. §1.469-4(f) gives the Commissioner regrouping power aimed at combinations built to manufacture material participation, and a missing Rev. Proc. 2010-13 disclosure lets an agent unwind the intended treatment without reaching the merits.
The election cuts both ways at exit — suspended losses stay locked until substantially all of the grouped activity is sold, so a grouping that helps this year can strand losses at disposition.
Grouping a rental with an operating business outside the insubstantiality or proportionate-ownership exceptions invites regrouping.
The §1.469-9(g) aggregation complicates property-level planning: one binding statement resets disposition timing and loss release for the entire portfolio.
stateNotes: Conformity: most states adopt federal AGI or taxable income and so conform to the federal §469 passive-loss architecture, meaning the grouping's federal effect usually flows through — verify separately in states that run their own passive limitations.
Missouri conforms through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121); the grouping requires no separate Missouri filing.

PTET interaction: none directly — grouping changes loss character at the owner level, not entity income, so there is nothing to model for PTET; confirm only that entity-level elections do not assume a different activity structure.
reviewChecklist: Grouping memo documents the five-factor economic-unit analysis and identifies the hours evidence it is meant to unlock.
Disposition modeling complete — the partner has seen the grouping's effect on suspended-loss release before filing.
Rev. Proc. 2010-13 disclosure (or §1.469-9(g) statement) drafted and attached to a timely return.
Prior-year filing positions reviewed for implied groupings that conflict with the new structure.
Client's time logs actually support material participation for the combined activity — the election reorganizes hours; it does not create them.

client.teaser: One election can add your work hours together instead of splitting them apart.
client.headline: Group related activities so your hours finally count
plainEnglish: Tax law sorts your income into two buckets: active and passive. Losses in the passive bucket cannot offset your regular income. Which bucket you land in depends on your work hours — counted one activity at a time.
Here is the catch. Spread your time across three related operations, and each one alone may miss the hour tests. All three get labeled passive, even though the combined work is your full-time job.

The fix is an election that treats related activities as one, so your hours add up. It moves no money by itself. But it can decide whether you use your losses this year or leave them stuck on a shelf. The choice binds future years, so we model the long-term effects first.
client.analogy: It is like three punch cards from the same shop. Merge them into one card, and your visits finally add up to the reward.
benefits: Hours across related activities count as one total
Can free stuck passive losses to offset your income
One filing with your return — no ongoing cost
steps: WE map each activity you own, who owns it, and where your hours go.
WE test which grouping unlocks the most losses now and at a future sale.
WE draft the election and required disclosure and file them with your return.
YOU keep a simple log of your hours so the combined activity holds up.
clientCommitments: Track your hours by activity as the year goes on
Tell us before you sell any property or business in the group — timing affects your locked-up losses

annualMaintenance: Re-confirm each year that the facts still match the documented economic unit
Verify material participation hours for the grouped activity each year
Review any acquisition or disposition against the binding grouping before it closes
deliverables: Grouping analysis memo documenting the five-factor test
Rev. Proc. 2010-13 disclosure statement (or §1.469-9(g) election) filed with the return
Disposition-impact summary for the client's permanent file
